--- title: "In-class_Ex06 : Emerging Hot Spot Analysis" author: "Xiaohan" date: "today" execute: eval: true echo: true freeze: true --- ## 1 Overview Emerging Hot Spot Analysis (EHSA) is a spatio-temporal statistical technique that identifies and categorises areas where clusters of high or low values of a phenomenon are developing, intensifying, or diminishing over time. It combines the Getis-Ord Gi\* statistic, which measures spatial clustering, with the Mann-Kendall trend test, a non-parametric trend analysis, to detect trends in these clusters within a "space-time cube" of data. The analysis consists of four main steps: - Building a space-time cube, - Calculating Getis-Ord local Gi\* statistic for each bin by using an FDR correction, - Evaluating these hot and cold spot trends by using Mann-Kendall trend test, - Categorising each study area location by referring to the resultant trend z-score and p-value for each location with data, and with the hot spot z-score and p-value for each bin. ## 2 Getting Started ### 2.1 Installing and loading the R packages `p_load()` of **pacman** package is used to check if the necessary packages have been installed in R; if yes, load them into the R environment. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} pacman::p_load(sf, sfdep, tmap, plotly, tidyverse, Kendall) ``` ::: ## 3 The Data Two data sets are used in this in-class exercise: - *Hunan*, a geospatial data set in ESRI shapefile format, and - *Hunan_GDPPC*, an attribute data set in csv format. ### 3.1 Importing geospatial data In the code chunk below, `st_read()` of **sf** package is used to import the *Hunan* shapefile into R. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} hunan <- st_read( dsn = "data/geospatial", layer = "Hunan") %>% st_transform(crs = 32650) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Reading layer `Hunan' from data source `/Users/wangxiaohan/ISSS626-GAA/In-class_Ex/In-class_Ex06/data/geospatial' using driver `ESRI Shapefile' Simple feature collection with 88 features and 7 fields Geometry type: POLYGON Dimension: XY Bounding box: xmin: 108.7831 ymin: 24.6342 xmax: 114.2544 ymax: 30.12812 Geodetic CRS: WGS 84 ``` ::: ::: ### 3.2 Importing attribute table In the code chunk below, `read_csv()` of **readr** is used to import *Hunan_GDPPC.csv* into R. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} GDPPC <- read_csv( "data/aspatial/Hunan_GDPPC.csv") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Rows: 1496 Columns: 3 ── Column specification ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────── Delimiter: "," chr (1): County dbl (2): Year, GDPPC ℹ Use `spec()` to retrieve the full column specification for this data. ℹ Specify the column types or set `show_col_types = FALSE` to quiet this message. ``` ::: ::: ## 4 Creating a Time Series Cube In the code chunk below, `spacetime()` of **sfdep** is used to create a spatio-temporal cube. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} GDPPC_st <- spacetime(GDPPC, hunan, .loc_col = "County", .time_col = "Year") ``` ::: Next, `is_spacetime_cube()` of **sfdep** package is used to verify if *GDPPC_st* is indeed a space-time cube object. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} is_spacetime_cube(GDPPC_st) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE ``` ::: ::: The **TRUE** return confirms that the *GDPPC_st* object is indeed a space-time cube. ## 5 Computing Gi\* Next, we will compute the local Gi\* statistics. ### 5.1 Deriving the spatial weights The code chunk below is used to identify neighbours and to derive inverse distance weights. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} GDPPC_nb <- GDPPC_st %>% activate("geometry") %>% mutate(nb = include_self( st_contiguity(geometry)), wt = st_inverse_distance(nb, geometry, scale = 1, alpha = 1), .before = 1) %>% set_nbs("nb") %>% set_wts("wt") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` ! Polygon provided. Using point on surface. ``` ::: ::: ::: callout-tip ## Things to learn from the code chunk above - `activate()` of **sfdep** package is used to activate the geometry context. - `mutate()` of **dplyr** package is used to create two new columns *nb* and *wt*. - Then we activate the data context again and copy over the *nb* and *wt* columns to each time-slice using `set_nbs()` and `set_wts()`. - Row order is very important, so do not rearrange the observations after using `set_nbs()` or `set_wts()`. ::: Note that this dataset now has neighbours and weights for each time-slice. ### 5.2 Computing Gi\* We can use these new columns to manually calculate the local Gi\* for each location. We do this by grouping by *Year* and using `local_gstar_perm()` of **sfdep** package. After which, we use `unnest()` to unnest the *gi_star* column of the newly created *gi_stars* data.frame. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(1234) gi_stars <- GDPPC_nb %>% group_by(Year) %>% mutate(gi_star = local_gstar_perm( GDPPC, nb, wt)) %>% tidyr::unnest(gi_star) ``` ::: ## 6 Mann-Kendall Test A **monotonic series** or function is one that only increases (or decreases) and never changes direction. So long as the function either stays flat or continues to increase, it is monotonic. - H0: No monotonic trend - H1: Monotonic trend is present **Interpretation** - Reject the null hypothesis if the p-value is smaller than the alpha value (i.e. 1 - confidence level). - Tau ranges between -1 and 1 where: - -1 is a perfectly decreasing series, and - 1 is a perfectly increasing series. ### 6.1 Mann-Kendall test on Gi\* With these Gi\* measures we can then evaluate each location for a trend using the Mann-Kendall test. The code chunk below uses Changsha county. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} cbg <- gi_stars %>% ungroup() %>% filter(County == "Changsha") %>% select(County, Year, gi_star) ``` ::: Next, we plot the result by using **ggplot2** functions. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(data = cbg, aes(x = Year, y = gi_star)) + geom_line() + theme_light() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](In-class_Ex06_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-9-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ### 6.2 Interactive Mann-Kendall plot We can also create an interactive plot by using `ggplotly()` of **plotly** package. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} p <- ggplot(data = cbg, aes(x = Year, y = gi_star)) + geom_line() + theme_light() ggplotly(p) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ### 6.3 Printing Mann-Kendall test report ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} cbg %>% summarise(mk = list( unclass( Kendall::MannKendall(gi_star)))) %>% tidyr::unnest_wider(mk) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 1 × 5 tau sl S D varS 1 0.485 0.00742 66 136. 589. ``` ::: ::: In the above result, **sl** is the p-value. If the p-value is smaller than 0.05, we reject the null hypothesis and infer that a monotonic trend is present; the sign of **tau** tells whether the trend is upward (positive) or downward (negative). ### 6.4 Mann-Kendall test data.frame We can replicate this for each location by using `group_by()` of **dplyr** package. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ehsa_mk <- gi_stars %>% group_by(County) %>% summarise(mk = list( unclass( Kendall::MannKendall(gi_star)))) %>% tidyr::unnest_wider(mk) head(ehsa_mk) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 6 × 6 County tau sl S D varS 1 Anhua 0.191 0.303 26 136. 589. 2 Anren -0.294 0.108 -40 136. 589. 3 Anxiang 0 1 0 136. 589. 4 Baojing -0.691 0.000128 -94 136. 589. 5 Chaling -0.0882 0.650 -12 136. 589. 6 Changning -0.750 0.0000318 -102 136. 589. ``` ::: ::: ### 6.5 Sorting to show significant emerging hot/cold spots ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} emerging <- ehsa_mk %>% arrange(sl, abs(tau)) %>% slice(1:10) head(emerging) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 6 × 6 County tau sl S D varS 1 Shuangfeng 0.868 0.00000143 118 136. 589. 2 Xiangtan 0.868 0.00000143 118 136. 589. 3 Xiangxiang 0.868 0.00000143 118 136. 589. 4 Chengbu -0.824 0.00000482 -112 136. 589. 5 Dongan -0.824 0.00000482 -112 136. 589. 6 Wugang -0.809 0.00000712 -110 136. 589. ``` ::: ::: ## 7 Performing Emerging Hotspot Analysis Lastly, we perform EHSA by using `emerging_hotspot_analysis()` of **sfdep** package. It takes a spacetime object x (i.e. *GDPPC_st*), and the quoted name of the variable of interest (i.e. *GDPPC*) for the `.var` argument. The `k` argument is used to specify the number of time lags, which is set to 1 by default. Lastly, `nsim` defines the number of simulations to be performed. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(1234) ehsa <- emerging_hotspot_analysis( x = GDPPC_st, .var = "GDPPC", k = 1, nsim = 99 ) ``` ::: ### 7.1 Visualising the distribution of EHSA classes In the code chunk below, **ggplot2** functions are used to reveal the distribution of EHSA classes as a bar chart. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(data = ehsa, aes(x = classification)) + geom_bar() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](In-class_Ex06_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-15-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ### 7.2 Visualising EHSA Before we can visualise the geographic distribution of EHSA classes, we need to join both *hunan* and *ehsa* together by using the code chunk below. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} hunan_ehsa <- hunan %>% left_join(ehsa, by = join_by(County == location)) ``` ::: Next, **tmap** functions are used to plot a categorical choropleth map. Only counties with statistically significant results (p-value \< 0.05) are coloured by their EHSA class. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ehsa_sig <- hunan_ehsa %>% filter(p_value < 0.05) tmap_mode("plot") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` ℹ tmap modes "plot" - "view" ℹ toggle with `tmap::ttm()` ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} tm_shape(hunan_ehsa) + tm_polygons() + tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) + tm_shape(ehsa_sig) + tm_fill("classification") + tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.4) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](In-class_Ex06_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-17-1.png){width=864} ::: :::
